evidence.title: Implementation of an artificial intelligence-based system for mammography in the compulsory medical insurance program: results of a 3-year study
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.outcome: technical error rates during monitoring

evidence.title: Monitoring Methodology for an AI Tool for Breast Cancer Screening Deployed in Clinical Centers
evidence.outcome: Output score distribution drift monitoring vs. pre-deployment reference, detection of mismatched configurations
evidence.effect: Matched-reference PCCs 0.975–0.998 with no significant chi-squared differences (p 0.346–0.853); unmatched references gave PCCs 0.364–0.825, showing the method flags deviations.
evidence.quote: The low PCC value found when an unmatched manufacturer is used for the reference shows that finding a difference could be the source of an alert, which would facilitate the detection of software malfunctions or deviations (such as an unsupported manufacturer or a version of the tool that is not suitable for the analyzed mammogram).

evidence.title: Detecting atypical alert behavior through statistical process control: Clinical decision support alert frequency visualizations
evidence.outcome: Detection of abnormal CDS alert behavior via SPC frequency dashboard
evidence.effect: From June-August 2022, SPC-flagged alerts with greatest variation were investigated and found to be functioning correctly; variation reflected practice changes rather than system errors. Authors call it time-efficient and effective.
evidence.quote: The most profound abnormalities detected during implementation reflected changes in practice and not system errors, though further investigation into thresholds for statistical significance will benefit this field.

evidence.title: Statistical process control for performance monitoring and continuous quality assurance of deep learning segmentations in radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Automatic detection of clinically significant segmentation performance deterioration
evidence.effect: Continuous monitoring detected a clinically significant humerus performance drop, reflected in 4 trend shifts after the software upgrade. Sensitivity and specificity were not tested.
evidence.quote: Although the current setup was not tested for sensitivity and specificity, with the integration of the CQA framework, a clinically significant performance drop of the humerus was detected automatically.

evidence.title: Establishing prospective performance monitoring for real-world implementation of deep learning-based auto-segmentation in prostate cancer radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Monthly monitoring of auto-segmentation agreement with clinical contours for drift
evidence.effect: Monthly monitoring detected model switch/practice change; no degradation trend or clinician overreliance observed over 20 months; authors recommend at least monthly QA.
evidence.quote: The monitoring system effectively detected out-of-distribution outliers and clinical practice changes, providing a reliable framework for early detection of monthly performance degradation.

evidence.title: Ensuring fair, safe, and interpretable artificial intelligence-based prediction tools in a real-world oncological setting
evidence.outcome: Detection of missing predictions
evidence.effect: Continuous monitoring identified a 2-week period with significantly lower prediction volume caused by EHR API connection issues.

evidence.title: Using a Large Language Model for Postdeployment Monitoring of FDA-Approved Artificial Intelligence: Pulmonary Embolism Detection Use Case
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR

evidence.quote: A 2% to 3% decline in model specificity caused a 2- to 3-fold increase in discrepancies, and a 10% drop in sensitivity was required to produce a similar effect.

evidence.title: Are Limited Electronic Medical Record Follow-Up Data Sufficiently Useful for Validating the Performance of Survival Prediction Models?
evidence.outcome: Whether EMR-only follow-up data can validate model discrimination and calibration versus registry-plus-EMR reference standard

evidence.quote: EMR data were useful for validation of model discrimination, but not calibration.

evidence.title: Importance of model governance in clinical AI models: case study on the relevance of data drift detection
evidence.outcome: Whether drift monitoring detects input distribution shifts and data quality problems in a deployed-style predictive model
evidence.effect: Univariate monitoring found respiratory rate shift from January 2022; multivariate PCA flagged three months, with data entry errors traced. Drift alerts did not coincide with the AUC dips in March 2020 and March 2021.
evidence.quote: In particular, multivariate monitoring surfaced data entry errors that were not detected by univariate methods and were absent from the training dataset, demonstrating how a comprehensive drift detection approach can uncover subtle or single-instance outliers.

evidence.title: ReclAIm: A Multi-Agent Framework for Monitoring and Correcting Performance Decline in Medical Imaging AI
evidence.outcome: Detection of performance decline between test and inference data by automated monitoring

evidence.title: Scalable Drift Monitoring in Medical Imaging AI
evidence.outcome: Whether drift detection signals correlate with imaging AI performance changes during COVID-19
evidence.effect: MMC+ detects significant data shifts that correlate with performance changes and indicates when AI systems may deviate from acceptable performance bounds; no numbers reported in abstract.
evidence.quote: Validated with data from Massachusetts General Hospitalduring the COVID-19 pandemic, MMC+ effectively detects significant data shifts that correlate with performance changes and indicates when AI systems may deviate from acceptable performance bounds.

evidence.title: Dynamic AI Risk Loop (DARL): A Continuous Risk Management Framework for AI-Enabled Health Information Systems in Medical Device Software
evidence.outcome: Early detection of simulated model drift by continuous drift detection layer
evidence.effect: DARL detected early-stage degradation at month 5, when sensitivity had declined by only 2.5 percentage points from the validated baseline of 94.0%, which complaint-driven surveillance would not flag.
evidence.quote: A 12-month simulation study, conducted under controlled synthetic drift conditions based on published AI benchmarks, demonstrates that DARL detects early-stage performance degradation at month 5, when model sensitivity had declined by only 2.5 percentage points from the validated baseline of 94.0%, a point at which conventional complaint-driven surveillance systems would not generate a structured risk signal.

evidence.title: A quality assurance framework for routine monitoring of deep learning cardiac substructure computed tomography segmentation models in radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of QA framework in monitoring domain shift and predicting autosegmentation performance
evidence.effect: QA framework predicted DSC with MAE 0.041 ± 0.002 for clinically anticipated abnormal domain shifts.
evidence.quote: A QA framework was able to predict cardiac substructure autosegmentation model performance for clinically anticipated "abnormal" domain shifts.

evidence.title: Empirical data drift detection experiments on real-world medical imaging data

evidence.effect: AUROC stayed relatively stable through the first COVID-19 wave, while TAE + BBSD detected the drift (with a delay). Aggregate performance metrics changed less than 3% under synthetic drifts.
evidence.quote: Our work has demonstrated that data-based approaches to drift detection can detect data drift (both natural and synthetic) in instances when monitoring model performance in aggregate cannot.

evidence.title: Distribution shift detection for the postmarket surveillance of medical AI algorithms: a retrospective simulation study
evidence.outcome: Detection rate of simulated distribution shifts (population and image quality) by deep-learning shift detection tests
evidence.effect: Classifier-based C2ST achieved perfect detection for quality and co-morbidity subgroup shifts at n=1000; only method detecting sex shifts (0.79 at 30,000 training images); type I error stayed near 5%.
evidence.quote: Classifier-based tests performed best overall, with perfect detection rates for quality and co-morbidity subgroup shifts at a sample size of 1000.

evidence.title: One-class support vector machines for detecting population drift in deployed machine learning medical diagnostics
evidence.outcome: Ability of unsupervised OCSVM monitor to detect simulated input population drift without ground-truth labels
evidence.effect: Sensitivity to drift decreased as overlap increased: inliers 27 (5% noise), 486 (10%), 851 (30%) of 10,000 each. Proof of concept on simulated data only.
evidence.quote: We hypothesised that increased noise would correlate with more OCSVM-detected inliers, indicating a sensitivity to population drift.

evidence.title: Detecting and Remediating Harmful Data Shifts for the Responsible Deployment of Clinical AI Models
evidence.outcome: Label-agnostic drift detection
evidence.effect: Detected shifts from younger age/admission source, community-to-academic transfer, and BNP/D-dimer changes.

evidence.title: Monitoring strategies for continuous evaluation of deployed clinical prediction models
evidence.outcome: Fidelity of post-deployment performance estimates to ground truth under feedback loops and drift

evidence.quote: Measured across accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, average precision, brier score, expected calibration error, F1, precision, sensitivity, and specificity, in the presence of feedback loops, Adherence Weighted and Sampling Weighted strategies have the highest fidelity to the ground truth classifier performance while standard approaches yield the most inaccurate estimations.

evidence.title: Evaluation and tuning of a commercial automated planning system for prostate radiotherapy

evidence.quote: Two process control metrics have been demonstrated to monitor the introduction of AI planning into routine practice to ensure that the real-world performance was consistent with that projected.

evidence.title: Detecting Performance Drift in AI Models for Medical Image Analysis Using CUSUM Chart

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: machine learning models and real-world interventions for magnetic resonance imaging appointment no-shows in a hospital setting

evidence.title: Implementation and prospective performance evaluation of an intraoperative duration prediction model using high throughput real-time data

evidence.title: Assessing Calibration and Bias of a Deployed Machine Learning Malnutrition Prediction Model within a Large Healthcare System

evidence.title: Longitudinal Changes in Diagnostic Accuracy of a Differential Diagnosis List Developed by an AI-Based Symptom Checker: Retrospective Observational Study

evidence.title: Performance Drift in a Nationally Deployed Population Health Risk Algorithm in the US Veterans Health Administration

evidence.title: Managing a "responsibility vacuum" in AI monitoring and governance in healthcare: a qualitative study

evidence.title: Multisite evaluation of prediction models for emergency department crowding before and during the COVID-19 pandemic

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-four studies suggest that monitoring methods can detect input shifts, technical failures, and performance drops in deployed or simulated AI, but most are simulations or descriptive reports, and none compares monitoring with no monitoring on patient outcomes. The hazard studies show that silent degradation occurs in real deployments, which supports the rationale for monitoring without showing that monitoring prevents harm.

perspectives.view: The only randomized trial (41625485) found no drift in 24 weeks, so it could not show detection. Real-deployment reports (42701602, 36836797, 41399697, 41488801) show monitoring flagged errors, mismatched configurations, and upgrade-related drops. Most other tests are level 4 or 5 simulations. In 42712319, drift alerts did not coincide with AUC dips. Certainty for detection is low.

In a simulation, a 2% to 3% specificity decline produced a 2- to 3-fold rise in discrepancies, while sensitivity had to fall 10% for a similar signal (40602699). A +20 mg/dL shift left AUROC unchanged but lowered sensitivity (42712297). A simulated monitor flagged a 2.5-point sensitivity loss at month 5 (PPR1238327). Single aggregate metrics may miss harmful degradation.

A statistical process control dashboard flagged alert variation that reflected practice changes rather than errors (38366366). Monitoring caught a two-week drop in prediction volume from EHR API failures (37349541). EMR-only follow-up data falsely suggested survival underprediction (42664478). Two qualitative studies found monitoring ad hoc and mostly manual (41023723, 40199833).

One simulation using retinal images with a racial and ethnic minority focus found that a classifier-based test detected quality and comorbidity subgroup shifts, and detected sex shifts at a rate of 0.79 (38724581). A label-agnostic method detected shifts in age and admission source (40465297). Neither study examined Medicaid, safety-net, or language-based subgroups.

FDA draft guidance calls for monitoring device performance and input changes, and an international discussion paper calls for specified analyses and thresholds to detect degradation. One deployment applied a 10% technical error threshold over 24 months and exceeded it in one period (42701602). No study tests whether regulatory requirements change monitoring quality.

In one simulation, CUSUM monitoring detected a 1.5 SD shift within an average of 5 days and produced about 293 days between false alarms (42449079). Unsupervised and label-agnostic monitors may reduce reliance on scarce outcome labels (40204747, 40465297). Interviewees reported that few institutions invest in structured oversight infrastructure (41023723).

A veterans' risk model's PPV fell 4.0% between 2016 and 2021, and a 0.34% rise in false positive rate corresponded to 18,288 additional false positives (40815520). Two surgical errors arose from AI that had not been updated for new lens types (39613452). No study shows that monitoring would have caught these problems sooner.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares monitored with unmonitored deployments on time to detection, time to correction, or patient harm. Prospective real-deployment studies should report the sensitivity and false alarm rates of monitoring methods, the staff time they require, and whether detected drift led to recalibration that changed outcomes.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only test with a population focus was a simulation using racial and ethnic minority retinal data (38724581). Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that published detection performance applies to their patients and may need subgroup-level monitoring.
